head: 094f0809f03efd218c6d10ae92d076332c2c0926
title: Starlette · WebSocket denial responses
overview: Send a custom HTTP error before accepting a WebSocket. Follow the response, state changes and tests.

steps.title: Reject with an HTTP response
steps.heading: A WebSocket request can fail before it opens.
steps.why: A rejected upgrade normally becomes HTTP 403. This PR lets an app choose a response such as 404 with a body, before accepting the WebSocket. Follow how that response reaches the test client.

notes.title: Public contract
notes.text: send_denial_response(response) requires a server extension. The documented unsupported case raises RuntimeError; it does not silently choose another response.

steps.check: Is the connection accepted before the denial response is sent?
steps.next: Move from the documented behavior to the method a caller uses; this is the reading order, not a runtime call.

steps.title: Enter the new method
steps.heading: A new method sends an HTTP response before accepting the connection.
steps.why: An app can pass a Response with its chosen status and body to the new send_denial_response method. It reuses the existing Response transmission logic. If the server lacks the required extension, the method raises RuntimeError.

notes.title: Check support and send the response
notes.text: The new method checks for websocket.http.response support before running the Response. Passing self.send routes the denial messages through WebSocket message-order validation, which the following steps examine.

steps.check: Which method receives the messages emitted by Response?
steps.next: The example test constructs a base Response. send_denial_response calls that object, so follow the base Response.__call__ implementation to message creation. Subclass overrides need separate inspection.

evidence.text: The test constructs a base Response and passes it to the denial-response method.
After checking extension support, this calls the supplied response object.
The base Response callable produces the start and body messages.

steps.title: Create ASGI messages
steps.heading: Previously HTTP-only event names now adapt to WebSocket requests.
steps.why: Response previously always sent http.response.start and http.response.body. For WebSocket requests, it now prefixes both names with websocket., allowing the same Response to send an HTTP denial response. Status, headers, and body are sent as before.

notes.title: Apply the prefix to both messages
notes.text: Both start and body messages gain the prefix required for a WebSocket denial response. For ordinary HTTP requests the prefix is empty, preserving the existing event names.

steps.check: Why would prefixing only the start message be insufficient?
steps.next: The response receives WebSocket.self.send as its send callback. The base Response sends its start message through that callback, so follow WebSocket.send to its state handling.

evidence.text: The third argument to Response is the current WebSocket send method.
The send argument receives the start message.
WebSocket.send handles the start message and enters the response state.

steps.title: Enter the response state
steps.heading: A denial response is a third path from CONNECTING.
steps.why: Before this change, the app could accept or close a connection while CONNECTING. It can now start a denial response, entering RESPONSE instead of CONNECTED.

notes.title: Add a denial-response state
notes.text: The new RESPONSE state represents sending an HTTP body without accepting the connection. Keeping it separate from CONNECTED lets the sender enforce the message order required for a denial response.

notes.title: Allow a denial response to start while connecting
notes.text: CONNECTING previously allowed only accept and close messages. Adding response-start and moving to RESPONSE prevents the existing validation from rejecting the new Response transmission.

steps.check: Does starting a denial response mark the WebSocket as accepted?
steps.next: Handling the start message sets the RESPONSE state. The base Response sends the body next, so follow the RESPONSE branch of the same send method.

evidence.text: The start message changes the connection state to RESPONSE.
After sending the start message returns, the body is sent through the same callback.
The next call handles the body and its completion in the RESPONSE branch.

steps.title: Finish the response body
steps.heading: The last body message closes the application state.
steps.why: The new RESPONSE branch allows only body messages after a denial response starts. It stays in RESPONSE while more_body=True and moves to DISCONNECTED on the final chunk. This lets the body finish before rejecting any further messages.

notes.title: Close when the body finishes
notes.text: An absent more_body defaults to False. The existing Response.__call__ sends a single body without that key, so its response can finish here. A second start message instead of a body is rejected with RuntimeError by the new branch.

steps.check: What keeps a multi-chunk response open between chunks?
steps.next: In the test path, the send callback supplied to the app queues messages, and the session receives from that queue. Follow the session entry code that passes the first message to denial-response handling.

evidence.text: The test session supplies its _asgi_send callback when running the app.
This test app passes its send argument to the WebSocket constructor.
WebSocket stores the supplied callback as _send.
The body message is forwarded through _send.
Messages sent by the app are placed on the test session queue.
receive takes a message or exception from that same queue.
On session entry, the first received message is passed to _raise_on_close.

transition.uncertainty: These excerpts show the test app and both ends of its callback/queue path. They omit the full TestClient app-wrapping and session-construction path, so the callback identity across that wiring is inferred. They do not establish a real network server’s transport behavior.

steps.title: Expose the rejected response
steps.heading: Tests can now inspect the denial status, headers, and body.
steps.why: The existing session raised a disconnect exception on websocket.close. It now also handles denial-response start messages, collects the body, and raises the new WebSocketDenialResponse exception. Callers can catch the failed connection and inspect its HTTP response.

notes.title: Add extension support to test connections
notes.text: Adding websocket.http.response to the test scope enables the new method in the in-process transport. It does not establish support in any deployed server.

notes.title: Collect the body in the new response branch
notes.text: The added branch reads chunks until more_body is false or absent and joins them. Tests can inspect the complete body, rather than just the last chunk, along with the status and headers.

notes.title: Add a response-shaped disconnect exception
notes.text: The new exception inherits from both httpx.Response and WebSocketDisconnect. It exposes HTTP response data and can also be caught by code that already handles WebSocketDisconnect.

steps.check: Where are multiple body chunks joined, and what stops that loop?
steps.next: After reading how the exception carries response data, inspect tests that check the status, headers, and body seen by the caller. This move follows the explanation rather than runtime order.

reference.label: Reference · session entry
reference.text: Session entry sends websocket.connect and passes the first server message to _raise_on_close. This is why denial raises while entering the context manager.

steps.title: Assert status, headers and body
steps.heading: New tests check delivery of both single and chunked bodies.
steps.why: The added assertions check that callers receive the denial status, headers, and body, including a body assembled from multiple chunks. Small ASGI apps use real Starlette response and WebSocket code with the in-process TestClient transport, rather than a live network server.

notes.title: Single response
notes.text: The app returns status 404 and foo. The test catches WebSocketDenialResponse at websocket_connect and asserts both status and body.

notes.title: Multiple chunks
notes.text: The first chunk says more_body=True; the second omits it. The caller must receive hardbody and the custom foo header.

steps.check: Which assertions would fail if the client kept only the last chunk?
steps.next: After the successful denial-response checks, compare failure cases for an unsupported extension and invalid message order.

steps.title: Check failure boundaries
steps.heading: Unsupported servers and duplicate starts are separate failures.
steps.why: One test removes extension support and expects RuntimeError; the app then closes the connection explicitly. Another sends two start messages and expects the response-state check to reject the second.

notes.title: No server extension
notes.text: The test removes the extension itself. send_denial_response raises; the later websocket.close() is a separate action by the app, not an automatic fallback.

notes.title: Start twice
notes.text: After the first start, the state expects a body. The test asserts the error describing the unexpected second start.

notes.title: Existing close behavior
notes.text: The existing close test now explicitly consumes the connection message, then still checks the original WebSocket close code.

steps.check: Can these in-process tests establish support in a real ASGI server?
steps.next: You have followed all five changed files. Revisit a step or open a definition to explore further.
recap: This walkthrough was checked against the pinned Git source.
The upstream Starlette test suite was not executed while creating this example.
Live ASGI server behavior is outside the checks shown here.

reference.label: Reference · existing close test
reference.text: The last line asserts the existing close code.

WebSocket.name: WebSocket
WebSocket.description: The complete connection wrapper. Its send method validates outgoing message order.

WebSocketState.name: WebSocketState
WebSocketState.description: The four application/connection states used by the WebSocket wrapper.

WebSocket.send.name: WebSocket.send
WebSocket.send.description: Validate outgoing messages and update application_state before forwarding them.

send_denial_response.name: WebSocket.send_denial_response
send_denial_response.description: Run a response through this WebSocket when the server advertises extension support.

WebSocketDisconnect.name: WebSocketDisconnect
WebSocketDisconnect.description: A disconnect exception carrying a close code and reason.

Response.name: Response
Response.description: The complete base response class. __call__ emits start and body messages; subclasses that override it must be considered separately.

Response.__call__.name: Response.__call__
Response.__call__.description: Emit status, headers and body using message names appropriate to the scope.

WebSocketDenialResponse.name: WebSocketDenialResponse
WebSocketDenialResponse.description: A test-client exception combining HTTP response inspection with disconnect handling.

raise_on_close.name: WebSocketTestSession._raise_on_close
raise_on_close.description: Convert ordinary closes or denial response messages into inspectable exceptions.

Scope.name: Scope
